item.title: Understanding Tax Residency for Foreigners in Cambodia
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
— And Why Declaration Is Essential

1. Who Qualifies as a Tax Resident?

According to Cambodian tax regulations, a foreign individual is considered a tax resident if they meet any of the following criteria:
  • Are domiciled in Cambodia, or
  • Maintain their principal place of abode in Cambodia, or
  • Are physically present in Cambodia for more than 182 days within any 12‑month period (CBRE, Moore Global).
Once classified as a resident, individuals are taxed progressively on their worldwide income, rather than at the flat 20% rate applied to non‑residents (CBRE). Tax brackets for residents (Salary Tax / Tax on Salary) include:
  • 0% on the first ~KHR 1.5 million/month
  • 5%, 10%, 15% on subsequent brackets
  • 20% on amounts above KHR 12.5 million/month (ASEAN Briefing, PwC Tax Summaries)
In contrast, non‑residents are taxed at a flat 20% on Cambodian‑sourced salary, with no allowances or deductions (CBRE).

2. Declaration of Residency: A Must, Not Automatic

It's important to understand that meeting the residency criteria alone doesn’t automatically change your tax treatment. Both the foreigner (employee) and the employer must formally declare and register the individual's tax residency status with the General Department of Taxation (GDT). This declaration is essential to activate the progressive tax system and access relevant benefits like deductions for dependents. Failing to declare can result in continued taxation at the higher flat rate, despite meeting residency thresholds. Moreover, both parties share responsibility for compliance (university.heavnn.io).

3. What You Should Do

If you're a foreign employee planning to stay in Cambodia long-term (ideally over 182 days in a 12-month stretch), here’s a simple checklist:
  1. Track your physical presence carefully—visas, entry/exit stamps, and rental agreements are handy evidence.
  2. Coordinate with your employer to file a formal tax residency declaration with the GDT.
  3. Ensure both you and your employer complete this process so the progressive tax regime applies moving forward.
  This dual declaration ensures you're properly classified as a resident for tax purposes—and ideally, taxed at the lower, more favorable progressive rates rather than the flat 20%.  

Summary Table

Status Tax Treatment Declaration Required?
Non-resident foreigner Flat 20% on Cambodian-source salary → No, unless applying otherwise
Foreign meeting residency criteria Progressive rates on worldwide income (0–20%) → Yes, both must declare

item.title: Is Cambodia Safe to Visit or Live In?
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
🇰🇭 Is Cambodia Safe to Visit or Live In? A Quick Update for Our Clients and Partners

Cambodia remains a safe and welcoming country for expatriates, tourists, and long-term residents.

While recent tensions along certain parts of the Cambodia–Thailand border have prompted precautionary advisories, daily life in major cities such as Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, and Sihanoukville continues as normal. Travel and work are unaffected, and there is no disruption to essential services.

As always, we advise our clients to: ✔️ Stay informed via local authorities and embassies
✔️ Avoid non-essential travel in isolated border areas
✔️ Register with consular services if staying long-term

At AG Cambodia, your safety and peace of mind are part of our commitment. Whether you're living here full-time or planning a visit, we're here to help you feel prepared and protected—with the right information and the right insurance coverage.

📩 Contact us anytime if you need advice, updates, or support.

#AGCambodia #CambodiaSafety #ExpatLife #TravelSafe #InsuranceCambodia

item.title: Work Permit & Business Visa?
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
What Expats in Cambodia Need to Know

(2025 Edition) If you're living in Cambodia as an expat — whether you're a freelancer, retiree with side income, or remote employee — you’ve probably asked yourself: “Do I need a work permit or is a business visa enough?” The short answer: both might be required, depending on your status and activity. Let’s break it down so you can stay compliant — and avoid fines or visa issues.

Visas: Your Entry Point

Most foreigners working or earning income in Cambodia enter with a Category E (EB) visa — commonly referred to as a business visa. This visa is not a work permit itself. It only gives you permission to stay in the country for work or business purposes.
Duration
  • Issued for 30 days initially
  • Can be extended for 1, 3, 6, or 12 months
  • Renewable without limit

Work Permits: Mandatory for Most Workers

A work permit is legally required in addition to your visa if you are employed or conducting business in Cambodia. Work permits are issued and managed online FWCMS Cost (official fee): $130 - Some agencies may charge you for their services.
What you need:
  • Valid passport and business visa
  • Proof of employment or business registration
  • Employer’s approval and quota compliance
  • Medical certificate
⚠️ Yes, even freelancers and remote workers need a work permit, unless exempt. More on that below.

What About Freelancers & Remote Workers?

Cambodia does not have a formal status for freelancers. If you're working independently (for clients abroad or locally), you are technically self-employed and must: ✅ Register a legal entity (e.g., sole proprietorship or company)
✅ Obtain a business visa
✅ Apply for a work permit under your own company Tip: If you invoice clients in Cambodia or abroad, and reside in the country long-term, you’re considered “working” — even without a local employer.

Retirees with Side Gigs — Are You Affected?

If you’re retired but:
  • Offer consulting services
  • Teach part-time
  • Run a YouTube channel or monetized blog
Then yes — Cambodian law may consider you economically active. You should look into:
  • Business visa
  • Work permit
  • Company registration (if relevant)
⚠️ However, pension income alone does not require a work permit.

Employed by a Local Company?

Your employer is responsible for:
  • Requesting a foreign worker quota (max 10% of workforce)
  • Registering you for NSSF (social security)
  • Applying for your annual work permit

What If I Don’t Get a Work Permit?

Penalties include:
  • Fines
  • Visa cancellation
  • Future visa complications
  • The government has been increasing enforcement, especially in Phnom Penh and Siem Reap.

Social Security Contributions (NSSF)

If you're employed (or run a business), you're also expected to register with Cambodia's National Social Security Fund (NSSF).

NSSF includes:

  • Health coverage

  • Work accident protection

  • Retirement contributions

📌 Employers must pay 100% of health coverage since 2018.
📌 Pension contributions started at 4% of salary (shared employer/employee).

Golden Visa: A Workaround?

If you're an investor, you may qualify for the CM2H Golden Visa:

  • $100,000+ investment = 10-year renewable visa

  • No work permit required

  • Citizenship possible after 5 years

This is ideal for passive investors or entrepreneurs seeking residency without formal employment.

              • Retirement contributions<\/p><\/li><\/ul>

                \ud83d\udccc Employers must pay 100% of health coverage since 2018.
                \ud83d\udccc Pension contributions started at 4% of salary (shared employer\/employee).<\/p>

                Golden Visa: A Workaround?<\/h2>

                If you're an investor, you may qualify for the CM2H Golden Visa<\/strong>:<\/p>

                • $100,000+ investment = 10-year renewable visa<\/p><\/li>

                • No work permit required<\/p><\/li>

item.title: Is Mandatory Third-Party Car Insurance Coming to Cambodia?
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
What It Means for Drivers

The Cambodian government is reportedly considering making third-party motor insurance mandatory for all vehicles. While this would represent an important regulatory shift for Cambodia, it is far from unusual. In fact, mandatory third-party liability insurance is the international standard in most countries around the world. So what would this mean for Cambodian drivers?

What Is Third-Party Insurance?

Third-party motor insurance covers damage or injury you cause to others while driving. It typically includes:
  • Injury or death of another person
  • Damage to another person’s vehicle
  • Damage to property (buildings, fences, etc.)
Importantly, it does not cover damage to your own vehicle. That would require comprehensive insurance.

Why Is It Mandatory in Most Countries?

In Europe, North America, Australia, and much of Asia, third-party liability coverage is legally required before a vehicle can be registered or used on public roads. The reason is simple: Driving creates risk — not only for the driver, but for everyone else on the road. Without mandatory insurance:
  • Victims may struggle to receive compensation
  • Drivers may face catastrophic personal financial liability
  • Legal disputes become longer and more complicated
Mandatory third-party coverage protects not only individuals, but also the broader economy.

What Could Change in Cambodia?

If implemented, mandatory third-party insurance could have several implications:

- Increased Protection for Road Victims

In the event of an accident, injured parties would have a clearer path to compensation.

- Greater Financial Responsibility

Drivers would no longer risk being personally exposed to large compensation claims.

- More Structured Road Risk Management

Insurance companies would play a larger role in accident handling and claims resolution.

- Administrative Adjustments

Vehicle registration processes may require proof of valid insurance.

Would This Increase Costs for Drivers?

Possibly — but third-party insurance is typically the most affordable form of motor coverage. In many countries, basic liability coverage costs a fraction of what a single accident could cost out-of-pocket. The real question is not the cost of insurance — but the cost of driving without it.

What This Means for Cambodian Drivers

If the regulation moves forward, drivers should: ✔️ Understand the minimum required coverage ✔️ Compare policy options carefully ✔️ Ensure policies are renewed on time ✔️ Consider whether comprehensive coverage might offer additional peace of mind For many, this may also be an opportunity to review their current level of protection — especially given the increasing number of vehicles on Cambodian roads.

A Positive Step Toward International Standards

Aligning with international practices would signal Cambodia’s continued modernization of its insurance and transport sectors. Mandatory third-party insurance is not about restriction — it is about shared responsibility and protection. At AG Cambodia, we support initiatives that improve transparency, safety, and financial protection for drivers and road users alike. If you have questions about how this potential regulation could affect you, our team is happy to guide you.

item.title: Health Insurance Cambodia Price: What to Expect in 2026
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
If you're living in Cambodia or planning to move here, one of the first questions you may ask is: How much does health insurance cost in Cambodia?

The short answer: Health insurance in Cambodia typically ranges from $600 to $6,000 per year depending on your age, coverage level, and provider.

But understanding what drives these prices, and what you actually get, is key to making the right decision.

You can listen to this article

Average Health Insurance Price in Cambodia

Health insurance prices in Cambodia vary widely depending on whether you choose local coverage or international coverage. But the age and the number of years one has been covered will greatly influence the cost of your insurance.

Here’s a general price guide:

  • It starts at around $600 per year for a young adult
  • And over $3,000 per year after 50 years of age.

Premiums will increase with age, but also prior coverage.

Local health insurance plans can sometimes be cheaper, but they often provide limited coverage, restricted hospital networks, or lower reimbursement limits.

Check out our instant form to get an idea of a price for you

Please enable JavaScript in your browser to complete this form.
Date of Birth *

Is Cheap Health Insurance Worth It?

Choosing the cheapest option is not always the best strategy.

Some low-cost plans may include:

  • Low annual limits
  • Limited hospital access
  • Exclusions for common conditions
  • Complicated claim procedures

Instead of focusing only on price, consider:

  • Coverage limits
  • Claims support
  • Hospital access
  • Emergency assistance

A slightly higher premium can sometimes make a big difference when it matters most.

How to Choose the Right Health Insurance

Here are a few simple steps:

  1. Define your budget
  2. Consider your age and health needs
  3. Decide where you want coverage
  4. Compare multiple insurers
  5. Ask about claim support

Working with an experienced insurance broker can also help you compare plans and understand differences clearly.

item.title: Car Insurance in Cambodia: Why Talking to a Broker First Might Be Your Best Move
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
Someone on Reddit put it well recently: *"I am not comfortable picking based off Google."* If you've just arrived in Cambodia and started poking around for car insurance, that probably resonates. It's not that the information isn't out there, it's that it's hard to know what to trust, or even what questions to ask. Insurance in Cambodia isn't as standardized as it might be back home. One policy might cover flood damage, another quietly excludes it. One insurer might process a claim in a week, another might leave you chasing them for months. Some third-party liability limits are so low they're almost not worth the paper they're printed on. You only find out which details matter when something goes wrong. And that's not a great time to be learning.

So why a broker?

The short answer is: they've already done the homework you'd otherwise have to do yourself. A broker works with multiple insurance companies, they're not tied to any one of them. Their job is to find the right fit for your situation, not to push a product. And despite what a lot of people assume, using a broker doesn't cost you more. They're paid by the insurer, not by you, so the price you get is usually the same as going direct — or sometimes better, because they can negotiate in ways you can't. More importantly, a good broker will ask you things you might not have thought to consider.
  • Do you drive outside Phnom Penh much?
  • Is your car new or older?
  • Is flooding a realistic risk where you park?
The answers actually change what coverage makes sense for you.

The part that matters most

Anyone can sell you a policy. What's harder to find is someone who picks up the phone when you've just had an accident on the side of a road in an unfamiliar country and you have no idea what to do next. That's where a broker earns their keep. They know the local claim procedures, they know which insurers are responsive and which aren't, and they can guide you through the process so you're not figuring it out alone. Car insurance is one of those things you buy hoping you'll never actually need it. But if you do need it, really need it, you'll be very glad you took a bit of time at the start to get it right. And in a new country, having someone in your corner from the beginning is worth a lot.

item.title: Understanding the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) in Cambodia
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
A Complete Guide for Employees, Employers, and Expats

The National Social Security Fund (NSSF) is Cambodia’s official social protection system designed to support workers and their families. While still developing, it plays an increasingly important role in the country’s healthcare, workplace safety, and retirement landscape.

Whether you are an employer, employee, or expatriate, understanding how the NSSF works is essential.

What Is the NSSF?

The NSSF is a government-managed social security system that provides basic protection to workers in Cambodia’s private sector. Its mission is to ensure access to healthcare, financial support in case of accidents, and long-term income security. (បេឡាជាតិសន្តិសុខសង្គម)

In simple terms, it functions as Cambodia’s national social insurance program — funded by contributions from employers and employees, and designed to protect individuals during times of need. (Premium Human Resources)

Who Is Covered?

The NSSF primarily covers:

  • Employees working in the formal private sector
  • Workers in registered companies
  • Increasingly, self-employed individuals and dependents (through newer voluntary schemes)

Employers with eight or more employees are required to register their staff with the NSSF. (PwC Tax Summaries)

The Three Main NSSF Schemes

The NSSF is built around three key pillars:

1. Health Care Scheme

This is the most visible part of the NSSF.

It includes:

  • Outpatient and inpatient treatment
  • Surgery and medication
  • Maternity care
  • Emergency services
  • Rehabilitation and physiotherapy

Workers also receive daily allowances (around 70% of wages) when unable to work due to illness. (បេឡាជាតិសន្តិសុខសង្គម)

Healthcare is provided through a network of approved public and private facilities.

2. Occupational Risk Scheme

This scheme protects workers in case of work-related accidents or injuries.

Benefits include:

  • Medical treatment
  • Temporary or permanent disability compensation
  • Survivor benefits for families
  • Funeral support

This ensures that employees are financially protected if something happens on the job. (Prake)

3. Pension Scheme

The pension system is a more recent addition and continues to develop.

It provides:

  • Old-age pension
  • Disability pension
  • Survivor benefits

To qualify for a pension, workers must contribute for a minimum period (typically several years). (Council for the Development of Cambodia)

This scheme aims to offer long-term financial security after retirement.

How Contributions Work

The NSSF is funded through mandatory contributions:

  • Occupational risk: ~0.8% (paid by employer)
  • Health insurance: fully paid by employer since 2018
  • Pension: shared between employer and employee

Contributions are calculated based on the employee’s salary and must be paid monthly. (PwC Tax Summaries)

 What Are the Benefits?

The NSSF provides several key advantages:

✅ Access to Healthcare

Workers can receive treatment at NSSF-approved facilities without paying full costs upfront.

✅ Financial Protection

In case of illness, injury, or disability, workers receive compensation or income support.

✅ Retirement Security

The pension scheme ensures some level of income after retirement.

✅ Social Stability

The system helps reduce poverty and improve workforce stability across the country. (International Labour Organization)

 

Limitations of the NSSF

While the NSSF is a major step forward, it is important to understand its limitations:

  • Coverage is mainly limited to Cambodia-based healthcare providers
  • Access to international hospitals is restricted
  • Benefits may not cover high-cost treatments abroad
  • The system primarily serves the formal sector, leaving many informal workers uncovered

This means that while NSSF provides a basic safety net, it may not be sufficient for all situations.

NSSF vs Private Health Insurance

This is a common question, especially among expatriates.

NSSF

  • Basic protection
  • Local coverage
  • Mandatory for employees
  • Limited international access

Private Health Insurance

  • Wider hospital access (including abroad)
  • Higher coverage limits
  • Medical evacuation included
  • Faster and more flexible claims

In practice, many individuals use both:

  • NSSF for basic coverage
  • Private insurance for comprehensive protection

What About Expats?

For expatriates:

  • If you are employed by a Cambodian company, NSSF registration is mandatory
  • If you are self-employed, participation may be optional depending on your structure

However, most expats still rely on international health insurance, as the NSSF does not cover:

  • Medical evacuation
  • Treatment outside Cambodia
  • High-end international hospitals

A System in Progress

Cambodia’s social security system has evolved significantly over the years. Initially introduced decades ago, it has been rebuilt and expanded to include healthcare and pension coverage for millions of workers. (បេឡាជាតិសន្តិសុខសង្គម)

Today, the NSSF continues to grow, with:

  • Expanded healthcare networks
  • Digital systems
  • New schemes for broader population coverage

Final Thoughts

The NSSF is a crucial foundation of Cambodia’s social protection system. It provides essential support for workers and represents a major step toward a more structured and secure healthcare environment.

However, it is important to see it for what it is:
👉 A basic safety net, not a complete solution

For many individuals — especially expatriates or higher-income professionals — additional private insurance remains essential to ensure full protection.

At AG Cambodia, we often help clients understand how NSSF fits into their overall protection strategy — and how to complement it with the right insurance coverage.

item.title: Foreigners Renting and Riding Scooters in Cambodia Without a Valid Motorcycle Licence
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
Executive Summary

For foreigners in Cambodia, the legal picture is narrower than the rental market makes it look. Under Cambodia’s Road Traffic Law, riders of motorcycles under 125cc do not need a Cambodian driving licence, but riders of 125cc and above do. Foreigners who lawfully live in Cambodia and wish to drive are directed by Article 45 to obtain a Cambodian licence unless a bilateral or multilateral recognition arrangement applies. In practice, this means the strongest legal position for a foreigner is either riding a sub-125cc scooter or converting a home licence into a Cambodian one through the Ministry of Public Works andTransport (MPWT).

The biggest risk is not just a police fine. It is the gap between what rental shops will hand over and what insurers or courts will recognize after a crash. Recent travel-advisory and insurer material shows that many hire companies have no insurance, travel insurers often restrict motorcycle claims unless the rider holds the correct motorcycle entitlement, and local motor policies commonly exclude driving “without a valid license” or, in one Cambodian insurer’s wording, without a valid Cambodian licence.

That means a foreigner can easily be rented a scooter that is easy to ride, easy to pay for, and hard to defend legally or financially after an accident.

Recent road-safety data underscore why this matters.

UNICEF Cambodia reports that road crashes in 2024 still caused 2,844 crashes, 1,509 deaths, and 3,720 injuries. In 2025 reporting, motorcyclists remained the overwhelming share of road deaths, and speed, right-of-way violations, wrong-side driving, and over taking were leading causes. For a foreign renter, the safest recommendation is simple: if you are not clearly licensed and insured for the bike you intend to ride, do not rely on the fact that a rental shop is willing to rent it to you.

Legal Baseline in Cambodia

Cambodia’s Road Traffic Law draws the central legal line at 125cc. Article 8 says drivers of vehicles with engine capacity from 125cc upward must hold a driving licence; for vehicles below 125cc, drivers are not required to hold a licence, though they must be at least 15 and carry an identity document. Article 40 places motorcycles from 125cc upward in Category A. MPWT’s public-service page also states broadly that every driver in Cambodia needs a valid licence, while its FAQ confirms that a car licence does not authorize a motorcycle above 125cc.

For foreigners who are resident

For foreigners who are resident rather than merely passing through, Article 45 is the decisive provision: unless Cambodia recognizes their licence through an agreement or international convention, foreigners lawfully living in Cambodia and wishing to drive must either take the Cambodian test or exchange their national licence through MPWT. The exchange requires a passport, valid visa, proof of address, medical 1 certificate, and an embassy-certified translation if the licence is not in English or French.

MPWT’s public-service centres include Aeon Mall Phnom Penh, Aeon Mall Sen Sok, provincial offices, and online intake through the driver-licence portal.

You can email them here: info@mpwt.gov.kh

  • Passport & Visa: Must be a valid "Ordinary" or Business Visa.
  • Proof of Address: A residence certificate or letter issued by your local Sangkat (commune) office.
  • Medical Certificate: A standard health check verifying fitness to drive (often obtained quickly at the MPWT public-service centers).
  • Translated Licence: If your home country's license is not in English or French, you must provide a translation certified by your embassy.
  • Passport Photos: Typically 3 white-background 4x6 cm photos (if applying in person). 

Penalties are less transparent in English than the underlying legal structure. Article 75 says driving without a licence triggers a provisional penalty under sub-decree, and repeated no-licence driving can escalate to criminal penalties for some drivers, but the law expressly says that the repeat-offender imprisonment clause does not apply to motorcycles, motorcycles with trailers, or tricycles. 

Separately, Cambodia’s demerit system deducts points for “failure to meet driving licence requirements,” and repeated use of an invalid or inappropriate licence can lead to larger deductions and eventual invalidity of the licence. The exact current roadside fine amount for motorcycle no-licence violations was not clearly available in the official English sources reviewed.

As an insurer broker, we need to remind everyone that even if your vehicle (motorbike or car) is insured, should you have an accident with an invalid driver's licence, the insurance will NOT cover you!  
Police powers are also narrower than many travelers assume.

The Road Traffic Law allows police to suspend licences in specified cases, keep vehicles after accidents, and temporarily keep certain vehicles for listed violations, but it also says police may not confiscate licences or vehicle papers outside the cases defined by law, and illegal confiscation by police is itself punishable. That matters because anecdotal reports of “bike confiscation” should not be treated as automatic or universally lawful for ordinary licence issues.

Police powers are also narrower than many travelers assume. The Road Traffic Law allows police to suspendlicences in specified cases, keep vehicles after accidents, and temporarily keep certain vehicles for listedviolations, but it also says police may
not
confiscate licences or vehicle papers outside the cases defined bylaw, and illegal confiscation by police is itself punishable. That matters because anecdotal reports of “bike confiscation” should not be treated as automatic or universally lawful for ordinary licence issues.
Recognition of Foreign Licences
The law itself does
not
publish a simple country-by-country list in English. Instead, it says recognitiondepends on bilateral or multinational agreements or international conventions. One treaty-level clue is theASEAN agreement on recognition of domestic driving licences, which states that ASEAN states recognizedomestic licences other than temporary, provisional, or learner permits. But public-facing guidance forforeigners remains inconsistent.
That inconsistency is important. The UK’s FCDO says that to hire a motorcycle
over 125cc
, travelers maysometimes need the
1949 International Driving Permit
plus their home licence, and that long-term rentalor private driving requires a Cambodian licence. By contrast, the Australian Embassy in Phnom Penh statesthat foreigners wishing to drive in Cambodia must hold a Cambodian driver licence and that internationallicences are not accepted, while also noting that no licence is required for motorcycles up to 125cc. Acommercial self-drive operator claims Cambodia accepts the 1949 IDP, but that is not the same as clear,official Cambodian foreigner guidance.
The safest analytical conclusion is this: for
sub-125cc scooters
, Cambodian road law itself is the strongestbasis for legality; for
125cc and above
, the strongest short-term documentary package reflected in currentEnglish-language guidance is a home motorcycle licence plus a
1949 IDP
, but enforcement and roadsideunderstanding may still be inconsistent; for
residents
, a Cambodian licence is the least contestable option.
The decision path below summarizes that logic from the cited legal and travel-advisory sources.
2
Rental Market Practice in Phnom Penh and Tourist Areas
The rental market clearly clusters around the legal threshold. Siem Reap rental sites prominently advertise
110cc and 125cc scooters, while also listing some 150cc models such as the Honda PCX 150. Another
Cambodia-based operator explicitly markets that no driver’s licence is needed for motorbikes under 125cc
and quotes deposits ranging from $300 to $900 depending on model. This pattern strongly suggests that
operators know the 125cc threshold shapes customer demand.
What shops actually check is often looser than the law. A recent Cambodia hostel guide wrote that smallscooter
rental is usually “pay, leave a passport copy or deposit, grab the key,” with no one asking about a
licence. Recent Reddit and Cambodia Expats Online discussions tell a similar story: tourists and expats
report that for small scooters, roadside attention is often more focused on helmets, mirrors, lights, and
obvious violations than on licence verification, especially in tourist-heavy areas such as Siem Reap. These
are anecdotal reports, not legal authority, but they align with the commercial rental behavior.
Insurance and Liability Exposure
Insurance is where informal practice turns into real financial exposure. Cambodia’s insurance framework
does provide compulsory motor third-party liability insurance, but the official insurance texts reviewed
apply that requirement primarily to business-use vehicles, commercial transport, company vehicles, NGO/
international-organization vehicles, and similar categories, not to every private scooter on the street. Travel

3

not
have insurance andthat riders may personally bear damage, loss, or injury-to-others costs after an accident.
Even when insurance exists, licence status matters. Etiqa Cambodia’s private vehicle policy excludes drivingwithout a valid licence, while Dara Insurance’s product summary excludes a driver who has no validCambodian licence. At the same time, Cambodian road law exempts sub-125cc riders from needing alicence. That creates a real ambiguity: a rider may be lawful under traffic law but still face an insurerargument that coverage fails because the rider lacked the insurer’s required licence status. For foreigners,that is a material risk, especially if their home licence does not include motorcycle privileges.
Liability to third parties is also not something to assume away. Cambodian insurance law requires insuredcommercial vehicles to compensate third parties for bodily injury or death, but if the rental bike isuninsured or the policy is voided or excluded, the rider can find the claim landing directly on them. TheRoad Traffic Law also places drivers under criminal law for driving-related offenses and vehicle ownersunder civil liability when their vehicles cause accidents.
Enforcement and Safety Risk
On enforcement, the most defensible conclusion is that Cambodia operates on a mix of
formal law
and
uneven roadside practice
. The FCDO notes on-the-spot helmet fines; Smartraveller says speeding ticketsshould be paid at payment centres and emphasizes that drivers should have a valid licence and confirmedinsurance. Recent forum reports suggest that in tourist zones, checks often target visible infractions first.That does
not
make no-licence riding safe; it means the legal and financial consequences often arrive onlywhen a crash occurs.
The safety backdrop is severe. UNICEF Cambodia reports that 2024 still saw
1,509 deaths
and
3,720
injuries
from road crashes. A 2025 road-safety profile put Cambodia’s road-fatality rate at
18.8 per 100,000
.In 2025 reporting, roughly three-quarters to four-fifths of road deaths were motorcyclists, and among killedmotorcyclists a large share were not wearing helmets. Recent local reporting attributes about half ofcrashes to speed, with right-of-way violations, wrong-side driving, and overtaking next. Night travel is alsorepeatedly flagged as higher risk.
Practical Guidance for Foreigners
If your nationality is unspecified, the most prudent advice is nationality-neutral. If you will ride
only a
sub-125cc scooter for a short stay
, you are on the strongest footing under Cambodian road law, but youshould still verify whether your
travel insurer
covers you for motorcycle riding and whether your homelicence gives you motorcycle entitlement. If you want to ride
125cc or above
, do not assume a rentalcounter’s willingness proves legality; carry a valid home motorcycle licence and, at minimum, the
1949 IDP
reflected in UK guidance, understanding that Australian guidance conflicts and roadside recognition mayvary. If you will
live in Cambodia and drive regularly
, exchange your licence or sit the Cambodian testthrough MPWT.
Do not leave your passport as a deposit unless you have no viable alternative and fully trust the operator;both UK and Australian travel advisories caution against it. Carry a helmet, your identity document, thevehicle registration card, the rental contract, and whichever driving document is strongest for your case. If
4
your need is transport rather than riding itself, ride-hailing services such as Grab and PassApp are availablein Phnom Penh, Siem Reap, and Sihanoukville and usually present a lower-risk option than self-riding.

The main uncertainty in this subject is not the

; that part of the law is fairly clear. The uncertaintylies in
foreign-licence recognition above 125cc
, the exact current roadside fine table in official English,and the mismatch between road-law legality and insurance wording. For that reason, the safest operationalrule is stricter than what many rental shops allow: rent only the smallest bike your licence and insuranceclearly support, or get the Cambodian licence first.

That creates a real ambiguity: a rider may be lawful under traffic law but still face an insurerargument that coverage fails because the rider lacked the insurer\u2019s required licence status. For foreigners,that is a material risk, especially if their home licence does not include motorcycle privileges.
    Liability to third parties is also not something to assume away. Cambodian insurance law requires insuredcommercial vehicles to compensate third parties for bodily injury or death, but if the rental bike isuninsured or the policy is voided or excluded, the rider can find the claim landing directly on them. TheRoad Traffic Law also places drivers under criminal law for driving-related offenses and vehicle ownersunder civil liability when their vehicles cause accidents.
    Enforcement and Safety Risk
    On enforcement, the most defensible conclusion is that Cambodia operates on a mix of
    formal law
    and
    uneven roadside practice
    . The FCDO notes on-the-spot helmet fines; Smartraveller says speeding ticketsshould be paid at payment centres and emphasizes that drivers should have a valid licence and confirmedinsurance. Recent forum reports suggest that in tourist zones, checks often target visible infractions first.That does
    not
    make no-licence riding safe; it means the legal and financial consequences often arrive onlywhen a crash occurs.
    The safety backdrop is severe. UNICEF Cambodia reports that 2024 still saw

Recent local reporting attributes about half ofcrashes to speed, with right-of-way violations, wrong-side driving, and overtaking next. Night travel is alsorepeatedly flagged as higher risk.
    Practical Guidance for Foreigners
    If your nationality is unspecified, the most prudent advice is nationality-neutral. If you will ride

Carry a helmet, your identity document, thevehicle registration card, the rental contract, and whichever driving document is strongest for your case. If

item.title: Heart Disease, Hypertension and Diabetes: A Growing Health Challenge in Cambodia
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
Cambodia is facing a growing health challenge that often receives less attention than infectious diseases. According to health experts, non-communicable diseases (NCDs) such as heart disease, hypertension, and diabetes are rising rapidly across the country and are becoming a major concern for both public health authorities and healthcare providers. These conditions are often referred to as "silent diseases" because they can develop gradually over many years without obvious symptoms. Many people only discover they have high blood pressure or diabetes after experiencing serious complications such as a heart attack, stroke, or kidney problems.

Why Are These Diseases Increasing?

Several factors are contributing to the rise of cardiovascular and metabolic diseases in Cambodia. Urban lifestyles have changed significantly over the past decade. Many people spend more time sitting at work, exercising less, and consuming diets that contain higher amounts of sugar, salt, and processed foods. At the same time, smoking and excessive alcohol consumption remain important risk factors for many adults. Health experts also point out that people are living longer than before. While this is a positive development, it naturally increases the likelihood of developing chronic health conditions that require ongoing medical care. Recent Ministry of Health figures show a significant increase in both diabetes and hypertension cases nationwide, highlighting the growing burden these conditions place on families and healthcare facilities.

What it says

  • Diabetes: 292,197 new cases in 2025, up 26.8 percent year on year.english.news
  • Hypertension: 451,009 cases in 2025, up 12.2 percent year on year.english.news
  • The same report also noted 25,481 cardiovascular disease patients treated and 1,091 deaths, plus 389,553 mental health illness cases in 2025.

The Connection Between Diabetes and Heart Disease

Many people think of diabetes as a condition that only affects blood sugar. In reality, diabetes and cardiovascular disease are closely linked. Individuals with diabetes are at a much higher risk of developing heart disease, stroke, and kidney disease. High blood sugar can damage blood vessels over time, while high blood pressure and elevated cholesterol often occur alongside diabetes, creating a dangerous combination for long-term health. This is why doctors increasingly encourage patients to view these conditions as interconnected rather than separate health issues.

Prevention Starts with Early Detection

The good news is that many cases of heart disease, hypertension, and type 2 diabetes can be prevented or managed effectively through early detection and lifestyle changes. Simple measures can make a significant difference:
  • Monitor your blood pressure regularly.
  • Check your blood sugar and cholesterol levels during routine health screenings.
  • Maintain a healthy weight.
  • Exercise regularly.
  • Reduce salt and sugar intake.
  • Avoid smoking.
  • Limit alcohol consumption.
  • Follow medical advice and prescribed treatments.
Regular health check-ups are especially important for adults over 40, individuals with a family history of cardiovascular disease, or those who have risk factors such as obesity or smoking.

Protecting Your Health and Financial Well-Being

Managing chronic diseases often requires long-term medical care, specialist consultations, diagnostic tests, and medication. Without proper planning, these costs can become substantial over time. Health insurance can help individuals and families access quality medical care, both in Cambodia and abroad, while reducing the financial impact of unexpected health issues. As Cambodia continues to develop, awareness, prevention, and early treatment will play a critical role in reducing the impact of heart disease, hypertension, and diabetes. Taking action today could help prevent serious health complications tomorrow.

item.title: How much is Car Insurance in Cambodia?
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
If you've recently bought a car in Cambodia, or you're planning to, you may be wondering whether car insurance is really necessary. The answer is simple: while insurance may seem like an extra expense, it can save you thousands of dollars when the unexpected happens.

Is Car Insurance Mandatory?

At the time of writing, private vehicle owners in Cambodia are generally not legally required to carry third party liability insurance. However, the government has announced plans to introduce compulsory third party insurance in the near future as part of broader road safety reforms. Regardless of the legal requirements, driving without insurance means you are personally responsible for paying for any damage or injuries you may cause.

How Much Does Car Insurance Cost?

Fortunately, car insurance in Cambodia is relatively affordable. As a general guide:
  • Third Party Liability Insurance: approximately US$50 to US$100 per year
  • Comprehensive Insurance: typically US$200 to US$800 per year, depending on your vehicle's value, age, and the level of coverage you choose.
For many insurers, comprehensive premiums are calculated at around 1.5% to 3% of the vehicle's insured value.

What Does Comprehensive Insurance Cover?

A comprehensive policy usually provides protection against:
  • Accidental damage to your vehicle
  • Theft
  • Fire
  • Damage to third party property
  • Bodily injury to third parties
  • Optional benefits such as roadside assistance, windscreen cover, and personal accident protection
Coverage varies between insurers, so it is always worth comparing policies before making a decision.

Is It Worth It?

Many drivers only think about insurance after an accident. Even a relatively minor collision can lead to expensive repair bills, medical expenses, or liability claims. If your vehicle is financed through a bank or leasing company, comprehensive insurance may also be required for the duration of the loan. For most drivers, paying a few hundred dollars per year is a small investment compared with the financial consequences of a serious accident.

Final Thoughts

Car insurance is not only about complying with regulations. It is about protecting yourself, your passengers, your vehicle, and your finances. Whether you drive a small city car or a premium SUV, choosing the right policy helps ensure that you are prepared for the unexpected. At AG Cambodia, we help individuals and businesses compare policies from leading insurers, understand the differences in coverage, and choose the protection that best suits their needs, rather than simply selecting the lowest premium.

item.title: Bringing Your Pet to Cambodia? Here's What You Need to Know
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
Moving to Cambodia with a dog or cat has become much easier in recent years. Modern veterinary clinics, imported pet food, grooming salons, and boarding facilities are now widely available in Phnom Penh and Siem Reap, making Cambodia an increasingly pet-friendly destination.

Before you travel, make sure your pet has all the necessary documentation, including a recent veterinary health certificate, proof of rabies vaccination, vaccination records, and an ISO-compatible microchip if required by your country or airline. It's also advisable to check the latest import requirements with the Cambodian authorities and your airline before departure.

Once you're settled, you'll find quality veterinary care, pet supplies, and a growing community of pet owners throughout the country. The biggest adjustment for most animals is Cambodia's tropical climate, so keeping pets cool, hydrated, and protected against parasites is essential.

Read more here: https://wondersofcambodia.com/life-bringing-your-pet-to-cambodia-what-future-residents-need-to-know/

What about pet insurance?

This is a question we receive from time to time.

At the moment, pet insurance is not available in Cambodia. Owners are responsible for veterinary expenses themselves, so it's worth budgeting for routine care and unexpected medical treatment when planning your move.

Don't forget your own protection

While your pet may not be insurable locally, you can protect yourself and your family. International health insurance, travel insurance, and comprehensive motor insurance can provide valuable peace of mind as you settle into life in Cambodia.

If you're planning a move to Cambodia and would like advice on your personal insurance needs, the team at AG Cambodia is always happy to help.

item.title: Having a Baby in Cambodia: What Parents Need to Know About Care, Costs, and Coverage
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
Cambodia has made remarkable progress in maternal health over the past two decades. But behind that national success story sits a very practical question for every expecting family: where you deliver, and how you're covered, still makes a big difference.

The good news: real progress

Cambodia's maternal mortality rate has fallen by roughly two-thirds since the mid-2000s, driven by expanded health centres, more skilled birth attendants, and stronger antenatal care programs. Nationally, the vast majority of births are now attended by a trained professional — a dramatic shift from a generation ago. Phnom Penh, in particular, has become a genuine option for high-quality maternity care. Private hospitals such as Royal Phnom Penh Hospital and Sunrise Japan Hospital now offer international-standard obstetric services, English- and French-speaking staff, and modern neonatal facilities — care that, twenty years ago, most families would have flown abroad for.

The gap that still matters

That said, the improvement isn't evenly spread. Access to skilled antenatal care and to health facilities for delivery remains far higher in Phnom Penh than in rural provinces, where distance, cost, and limited infrastructure still keep many mothers from receiving regular check-ups or delivering with a trained attendant nearby. For families living or working outside the capital, planning ahead — choosing where to deliver, and how to get there safely — is not a formality; it's part of a real decision.

What it costs, and why timing matters

Private maternity care in Phnom Penh is genuinely good value by international standards, but it isn't free of surprises:
$500–1,500 Natural delivery
$800–3,000 C-section
$600–1,200 Antenatal package
$1,000–4,000 Full uncomplicated journey
Complications: an unplanned C-section, a NICU stay, an emergency transfer, can push costs well beyond $30,000, and in a serious case, medical evacuation to Bangkok or Singapore can add $2,000–5,000 more.
Most international health policies apply a 10–12 month maternity waiting period. In plain terms, coverage has to be in place before conception, not after a pregnancy is confirmed. Families who wait until they're expecting often find the door has already closed for that pregnancy.

What the law provides for working mothers

Cambodia's Labour Law also offers meaningful protection for employees:
  • 90 days of paid maternity leave, which can be taken before or after birth.
  • 50% of wages paid by the employer, now required to be paid in full and in advance of leave starting.
  • An additional 70% from the National Social Security Fund (NSSF) for employees with sufficient contribution history — meaning a compliant, tenured employee can receive up to 120% of her normal wage during leave.
  • Job protection: employers cannot dismiss a woman during maternity leave, or time a notice period to fall within it.
  • Paid breastfeeding breaks (one hour a day) for up to a year after birth.
These are strong protections on paper. But NSSF benefits, employer obligations, and private hospital costs are three separate systems — and a family's actual out-of-pocket exposure depends on how well they interact.

The takeaway

Cambodia offers real, high-quality options for pregnancy and delivery, but the safety net has gaps, and the financial risk of complications is not small. Whether you're an employer structuring benefits for your team, or a family planning ahead, the right time to think about maternity coverage is well before the test comes back positive.
AG Insurance Broker Cambodia has supported individuals, families, and companies across the Kingdom for nearly 20 years, helping clients navigate exactly these kinds of decisions, from choosing the right maternity coverage to understanding what local labour law and NSSF benefits actually provide. Get in touch with our team to talk through your options.

item.title: Renting a Home in Phnom Penh: What Tenants and Landlords Should Know
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
Written in collaboration with Phnom Penh Real Estate

Renting a Home in Phnom Penh: What Tenants and Landlords Should Know

Cambodia's rental market has matured fast. Whether you're an expat looking for a serviced apartment near the riverside, a family renting a villa in Toul Kork, or a local landlord letting out a unit for the first time, a smooth rental starts with knowing a few basics — long before you sign anything. Get everything in writing. A verbal agreement, even with a trusted contact, isn't enough. A proper lease should spell out the monthly rent, deposit amount, payment schedule, minimum lease term, notice period, and who's responsible for what (utilities, internet, minor repairs, pest control). In Cambodia, one to two months' deposit is standard, and it should always be returned in full at move-out if the property is left in good condition — normal wear and tear excluded. Document the property's condition. Before moving in, walk through with the landlord or agent and photograph everything: appliances, walls, plumbing, air-con units. This protects both sides when it's time to settle the deposit later. It's a five-minute habit that prevents most disputes. Know who fixes what. A common source of friction is maintenance. Generally, landlords cover structural issues and major appliance failures, while tenants handle day-to-day upkeep. Get this split written into the lease rather than assumed. Understand the renewal terms. Many leases in Phnom Penh run 12 months with an option to renew. Check the notice period required if either side wants to end the lease early, and clarify whether rent can be adjusted at renewal. For landlords: vet your tenants and protect your asset. A short reference check and a clear lease go a long way. It's also worth thinking beyond the lease itself — a rented-out property still needs protection against fire, water damage, or liability if something goes wrong while someone else is living in it. That's a separate conversation from the lease, but an important one for any landlord to have. Whether you're renting your first apartment or listing a property for the tenth time, working with an established local platform and putting the right paperwork in place makes the process far less stressful for everyone involved.
This article was written in collaboration with Phnom Penh Real Estate, Cambodia's largest property platform for renting, buying, and selling apartments and houses across Phnom Penh, Sihanoukville, Kep, Kampot, and Siem Reap. Browse current rental listings at phnompenhrealestate.net.

item.title: Cambodia Visa Guide 2026: Tourist, Business, Retirement and Long-Stay Visas Explained
item.dc:creator: agadmin
item.content:encoded:
This Cambodia visa guide 2026 explains everything tourists, expatriates, retirees and business professionals need to know about entering and staying in Cambodia. Discover the different visa types, application procedures, extensions, electronic arrival requirements and practical advice for living in Cambodia.

Do You Need a Visa to Enter Cambodia?

Most foreign nationals need a visa to enter Cambodia. However, some passport holders benefit from visa-exemption arrangements, particularly citizens of certain ASEAN countries. The permitted visa-free stay depends on nationality and the applicable agreement. Before traveling, check the latest requirements for your passport, including the permitted length of stay and any applicable electronic arrival procedures.

Cambodia Tourist Visa (T-Class)

The tourist visa is designed for visitors traveling to Cambodia for holidays, sightseeing or short personal visits.
  • Initial permitted stay: generally 30 days.
  • Entry: normally single entry.
  • Official e-Visa fee: USD 30.
  • Visa validity before entry: generally three months from issuance.
  • Extension: generally one additional 30-day extension.
A tourist visa is not intended for employment or long-term residence. Anyone considering a longer stay should investigate the ordinary visa category before arriving.

Cambodia Ordinary Visa (E-Class)

The ordinary E-class visa is commonly used by foreigners planning to stay in Cambodia for business, employment, retirement, education or other eligible purposes. An initial E-class visa generally allows a 30-day stay. The official e-Visa application fee is USD 35. Depending on the applicant's circumstances, an appropriate extension may be available after arrival. The E-class visa is sometimes informally called a business visa, but the extension categories serve different purposes.

EB Extension: Business and Employment

The EB extension is commonly used by foreign nationals working or conducting business in Cambodia. Supporting documentation may be required, including evidence of employment or business activity. An EB extension does not automatically replace the work permit or other employment-related authorizations that may be required under Cambodian law.

ER Extension: Retirement

The ER extension is intended for eligible retirees who wish to live in Cambodia without working. Applicants may need to demonstrate their retirement status and provide other supporting documents. This category is particularly relevant to foreigners considering Cambodia as a long-term retirement destination.

ES Extension: Study

The ES extension is designed for eligible foreign students studying in Cambodia. Proof of enrollment or documentation from an educational institution may be required.

EG Extension: General or Job-Seeking Purposes

The EG extension is commonly associated with foreign nationals exploring employment opportunities or making arrangements for their next steps in Cambodia. Eligibility, duration and documentation requirements should be confirmed before applying. Extension periods and multiple-entry privileges vary by category. Approval is not automatic.

Cambodia K-Class Visa for People of Cambodian Origin

The K-class visa is intended for eligible people of Cambodian origin who hold foreign passports. It can be especially useful for members of the Cambodian diaspora returning to visit family or spend time in Cambodia. Applicants may need to provide documentation demonstrating Cambodian birth, ancestry or another qualifying connection. Requirements and application procedures should be confirmed with the relevant Cambodian embassy or consulate.

How to Apply for a Cambodia Visa

Depending on nationality and visa category, travelers may have several ways to obtain a Cambodian visa.

Applying Online Through the Cambodia e-Visa System

Cambodia's official e-Visa platform allows eligible travelers to apply electronically before departure. The general application process involves selecting the visa category, entering passport details, uploading the required documents, paying the applicable fee and downloading the approved electronic visa certificate. Standard tourist and ordinary e-Visa applications generally have a published processing time of approximately three business days, although travelers should apply earlier whenever possible. Visit the official Cambodia e-Visa website.

Visa on Arrival

Eligible travelers may obtain a visa on arrival at designated Cambodian international entry points. Availability depends on nationality, visa category and the specific airport or border crossing. Travelers should confirm eligibility before departure rather than assuming that visa-on-arrival services are available at every entry point.

Applying Through an Embassy or Consulate

Cambodian diplomatic missions remain important for special visa categories and applicants with circumstances requiring additional documentation. Cambodia has been expanding electronic visa procedures. Travelers should confirm the current application and issuance process with the relevant embassy or consulate, particularly for special visa categories.

Cambodia e-Arrival: What Travelers Need to Know

The Cambodia e-Arrival system is a digital arrival declaration. It is separate from the visa application process and does not itself grant permission to enter Cambodia. Travelers should complete the applicable e-Arrival formalities within the seven days before arrival, following the latest instructions for their entry point. The official e-Arrival service is free. Travelers should be cautious of unofficial websites that charge unnecessary processing fees. Access the official Cambodia e-Arrival website.

Understanding Cambodia's Digital v-Pass

Cambodia has introduced digital immigration records through its v-Pass system, replacing traditional passport entry and exit stamps for applicable airport and seaport procedures. The v-Pass records important immigration information, including entry details and the authorized period of stay. Travelers should retain access to this information and check it carefully after entering Cambodia. The v-Pass is not a visa. It is an electronic immigration record and should not be confused with either the e-Visa or the e-Arrival declaration.

Entering Cambodia by Air or Land

Cambodia has several international airports and land border crossings. However, not every entry point necessarily accepts every type of electronic visa. Travelers using an e-Visa should consult the official government's accepted-entry-point list before booking flights or planning an overland journey. This is particularly important for visitors traveling between Cambodia and neighboring countries, where border procedures and operational arrangements may change.

Working in Cambodia: Visa and Work Permit Requirements

Foreigners planning to work in Cambodia should understand that immigration permission and employment authorization are separate matters. A visa or visa extension governs entry and residence, while work permits and labor-related registration are subject to separate requirements. Employees and business owners should confirm their obligations with the appropriate Cambodian authorities or qualified professional advisers.

Extending Your Cambodian Visa

Visa extensions should be arranged before the authorized stay expires. The appropriate extension depends on the visa category, the purpose of residence and the applicant's supporting documents. Some extensions may allow longer stays and multiple entries, while others are more limited. Applicants should confirm the current rules, documentation requirements and fees before submitting an extension request. Travelers should also distinguish between a visa's validity for entry and the permitted duration of stay granted by immigration authorities.

What Happens If You Overstay Your Visa?

Remaining in Cambodia beyond the authorized period can lead to overstay penalties and potentially more serious immigration consequences. Travelers should check their permitted stay after arrival and arrange extensions well before the expiration date. The expiry date of an e-Visa certificate is not necessarily the same as the final day of the authorized stay.

Practical Checklist Before Traveling to Cambodia

  • Check that your passport has sufficient remaining validity, generally more than six months at entry.
  • Confirm the visa requirements for your nationality.
  • Choose the visa category appropriate to your travel purpose.
  • Apply through official government websites when using online services.
  • Confirm that your intended entry point accepts your visa type.
  • Complete the applicable e-Arrival declaration.
  • Keep electronic copies of your passport, visa and travel documents.
  • Check your authorized stay and plan extensions in advance.
  • Confirm work-permit requirements if relocating for employment.
  • Review your health insurance and medical evacuation coverage before traveling.

Our Cambodia visa guide 2026 covers the most common questions about visa extensions, long-term residence and electronic immigration procedures. Understanding these requirements can help visitors and expatriates prepare for their stay.

Frequently Asked Questions About Cambodia Visas

Can I stay long-term in Cambodia on a tourist visa?

Tourist visas are intended for short visits and offer limited extension options. Foreigners planning to remain longer should investigate an appropriate ordinary visa and extension category.

Can I apply for a Cambodian visa online?

Yes. Eligible applicants can use the official Cambodia e-Visa portal. Available visa categories and supporting documentation depend on the application.

Is the Cambodia e-Arrival declaration the same as an e-Visa?

No. An e-Visa provides visa authorization, while e-Arrival is a separate digital arrival declaration. Travelers may need to complete both processes.

Can foreigners retire in Cambodia?

Eligible foreign retirees may qualify for an ER extension of an ordinary visa, subject to the current immigration requirements and supporting documentation.

Does an ordinary visa automatically allow employment?

No. An ordinary visa or EB extension does not automatically replace applicable work-permit and labor requirements.

Can I leave Cambodia and return on the same visa?

Standard tourist and ordinary e-Visas are generally single-entry visas. Certain longer-term extensions may offer multiple-entry privileges. Travelers should check their specific visa conditions before leaving Cambodia.

Moving to Cambodia? Don't Forget Health Insurance

Obtaining the correct visa is only one part of preparing for life in Cambodia. Foreigners planning to relocate should also consider their healthcare arrangements, especially if they intend to remain for several months or years. Private health insurance can help with the cost of medical treatment, hospitalization and other healthcare needs. International plans may also provide access to treatment outside Cambodia and emergency medical evacuation, depending on the policy. Established in 2006, AG Cambodia is an insurance broker helping expatriates, families and businesses explore insurance solutions for living and working in Cambodia. Discover insurance solutions with AG Cambodia.

Official Cambodia Visa Resources

  • Official Cambodia e-Visa Portal
  • Official Cambodia e-Arrival Portal
We hope this Cambodia visa guide 2026 helps you prepare for your visit or relocation. As immigration regulations can change, always confirm the latest requirements with the relevant Cambodian authorities.

Conclusion

Cambodia offers visa options for tourists, professionals, students, retirees and eligible people of Cambodian origin. Understanding the differences between these categories helps travelers make informed decisions and avoid unnecessary administrative difficulties. As Cambodia continues to modernize its immigration procedures, visitors should also understand the distinction between electronic visas, digital arrival declarations and electronic entry records. Before traveling or relocating, always check the latest official requirements and make sure your immigration and insurance arrangements are appropriate for your circumstances. Disclaimer: This article provides general information and does not constitute immigration or legal advice. Visa rules, fees, eligibility and extension procedures may change. Confirm current requirements with the relevant Cambodian authorities. AG Cambodia is an insurance broker, not a visa-issuing authority.
